meta.description: Deming really wrote it. The line appears in The New Economics for Industry, Government, Education (1993), his final book — with the edition and page verified.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A system must have an aim. Without an aim, there is no system'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: W. Edwards Deming wrote it in The New Economics (1993), his last book. Page 36 in the MIT Press third edition — not a paraphrase, not a fake.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Deming wrote it in The New Economics for Industry, Government, Education, his final book, first published in 1993 by MIT’s Center for Advanced Engineering Study. The sentence sits inside his definition of a system, and the wording that circulates online is his, not a paraphrase — the W. Edwards Deming Institute ↗ quotes it verbatim and puts it on p. 36 of the 2018 MIT Press third edition.

source.excerpt: A system is a network of interdependent components that work together to try to accomplish the aim of the system. A system must have an aim. Without an aim, there is no system.
trail: The book is real and datable: the Internet Archive catalogue record ↗ shows The new economics for industry, government, education by W. Edwards Deming (1900–1993), published 1993 by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Center for Advanced Engineering Study, ISBN 9780911379051.
Wikiquote ↗ carries the sentence inside its longer paragraph, in the Quotes section under the heading for the 1993 book — not in the page’s separate Misattributed section.

The W. Edwards Deming Institute ↗ publishes the exact wording with the citation “Deming, W. Edwards. (2018). The New Economics for Industry, Government, Education – 3rd Edition. Kindle Edition. MIT Press,” page 36.
An independent reproduction of the same paragraph by Vanguard Consulting ↗ cites p. 50 of the 1994 MIT edition, matching the wording exactly across two different printings.
source.cutTag: The New Economics, on the nature of a system
source.excerptNote: Deming’s paragraph continues past this point, adding that the aim must be clear to everyone inside the system, that it must include plans for the future, and that choosing it is a value judgment. Only the opening is reproduced here; the book is still in copyright and in print.

author.name: W. Edwards Deming
author.heading: W. Edwards Deming
author.metaLine: 1900–1993 · American statistician, engineer and management consultant
author.bio: W. Edwards Deming was an American statistician who spent decades arguing that quality problems are almost never the fault of the worker — they are baked into the system the worker is handed. His statistical methods helped rebuild Japanese manufacturing after 1945, and by the 1980s American executives were queuing for his four-day seminars. The New Economics, published in 1993, the year he died at ninety-three, set out his System of Profound Knowledge, whose very first component is “appreciation for a system.”

misattribution.heading: The Deming problem runs the other way
misattribution.intro: This one is real. That is worth saying plainly, because Deming is among the most heavily counterfeited names in management writing — crisp, systems-flavoured aphorisms get pinned on him constantly, and the two below are the ones you are most likely to meet in the same slide deck as the genuine sentence.

items.who: Arthur Jones, adapted by Paul Batalden
items.why: “Every system is perfectly designed to get the results it gets” is routinely credited to Deming. The Institute for Healthcare Improvement ↗ traces it to Arthur Jones, a Procter & Gamble colleague who said “All organizations are perfectly designed to get the results they get,” which Paul Batalden then adapted for healthcare. Deming’s thinking influenced both men; the sentence is not his.

“In God we trust. All others must bring data.” Wikiquote ↗ files it under Misattributed, noting an earliest attestation of 1978 and that it appears in Mary Walton’s The Deming Management Method (1986), p. 96 with no attribution to Deming or anyone else.

misattribution.truthLine: The aim-of-a-system sentence is not one of the strays. Wikiquote ↗ places it in its Quotes section under The New Economics (1993), and the Deming Institute ↗ quotes it word for word with an edition and a page number.

context.heading: Why Deming bothered to say something so obvious
lead: Deming was not making a motivational point. He was closing a loophole. By 1993 he had watched decades of managers announce “systems thinking” while running departments as rival profit centres, each optimising its own numbers. His answer was definitional: a collection of parts only becomes a system when a shared aim binds them, and if you cannot state the aim, you do not have a system to manage — you have components competing.

The sentence appears early in The New Economics, the book that set out his System of Profound Knowledge. It was published in 1993, the year Deming died, and it is the last extended statement of his thinking. Read in place, the line is a test you are meant to apply to your own organisation, not a slogan for a wall.
detailsBody: The quote turns up cited to two different pages, and both are right. Vanguard Consulting reproduces the surrounding paragraph and cites p. 50 of the 1994 MIT edition; the W. Edwards Deming Institute cites p. 36 of the 2018 MIT Press third edition. The book has been reset across editions, so the pagination moved while the wording did not.

Deming’s own paragraph does not stop at this sentence. It goes on to require that the aim be clear to everyone inside the system, that it include plans for the future, and it concedes that choosing an aim is a value judgment rather than a technical calculation.

sourcesVerified.claim: The W. Edwards Deming Institute publishes the exact wording "A system must have an aim. Without an aim, there is no system." and cites Deming, W. Edwards (2018), The New Economics for Industry, Government, Education – 3rd Edition, Kindle Edition, MIT Press, page 36.

Wikiquote carries the sentence inside the paragraph beginning "A system is a network of interdependent components..." in its Quotes section under the heading for The New Economics for Industry, Government, Education (1993); the page's separate Misattributed section contains only "In God we trust. All others must bring data.", noted as earliest attested 1978 and appearing in Mary Walton's The Deming Management Method (1986), p. 96 without attribution.

Edwards (William Edwards), 1900-1993; publisher Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Center for Advanced Engineering Study, Cambridge, MA; publication year 1993; ISBN 0911379053 / 9780911379051; 240 pages.

Vanguard Consulting reproduces the passage verbatim ("A system is a network of interdependent components that work together to try to accomplish the aim of the system. A system must have an aim. Without an aim, there is no system. The aim of the system must be clear to everyone in the system. The aim must include plans for the future. The aim is a value judgment...") citing Deming WE 1994, The New Economics: For Industry, Government, Education, MIT Press, p. 50.

The Institute for Healthcare Improvement states that "Every system is perfectly designed to get the results it gets" originated with Arthur Jones, a Procter & Gamble colleague, who said "All organizations are perfectly designed to get the results they get," and was adapted by Paul Batalden for healthcare; the article does not attribute the sentence to W. Edwards Deming.

W. Edwards Deming lived 14 October 1900 – 20 December 1993, was an American statistician, engineer, management consultant and writer, and The New Economics for Industry, Government, Education (1993) was his final book, containing the System of Profound Knowledge.

The third edition of The New Economics was released by MIT Press with a new introduction by Kevin Cahill, Executive Director of The W. Edwards Deming Institute and Deming's grandson, and the chapters written by Deming remain as he wrote them.

An independent reproduction of the same passage — "A system is a network of interdependent components that work together to try to accomplish the aim of the system. A system must have an aim. Without an aim, there is no system. The aim of the system must be clear to everyone in the system." — attributed to Deming's The New Economics.
